title: Esau runs to meet him (Genesis 33:1–11)
hookLine: Jacob fears revenge, but his brother runs, embraces him, and weeps
carry: to see your face is like seeing god

cards: Morning. Jacob is limping. He looks up, and there it is, the thing he has dreaded for twenty years: Esau, coming with four hundred men.
Jacob lines up his family, the servants and their children in front, Leah and hers next, Rachel and little Joseph at the very back, where they'll be safest.
Then he walks out ahead of them all, alone, and bows to the ground seven times, each bow a little closer.
Everyone has a version of this walk: the call you've avoided, the person you wronged, coming toward you, and you can't read their face.

teach.b: And then Esau runs. In the King James Bible: "And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept." No speech.
No list of grievances. The brother who once said he would kill Jacob runs to him. Genesis doesn't explain what changed in Esau, whether he forgave slowly over twenty years or all at once on the road.
The silence is part of the gift. Jacob keeps pressing his herds on him.

Esau says, "I have enough, my brother; keep that thou hast unto thyself." Jacob insists, and says the line behind today's carry: "I have seen thy face, as though I had seen the face of God, and thou wast pleased with me."
Yesterday Jacob named the river Peniel, face of God, because he wrestled there and lived.

teach.h: GOD'S FACE IN A BROTHER'S FACE.
teach.b: Now he sees God's face again, in a brother's face he expected to be furious and found full of welcome. Christian readers often hear another story inside this one.
When Jesus tells of the prodigal son, the father sees his son far off, runs, falls on his neck, and kisses him: almost the same words. Many hear the father in Esau.

teach.h: AS THOUGH I HAD SEEN THE FACE OF GOD.
teach.b: And the story stays honest. The brothers don't move in together. They part kindly and live in different places.
Reconciliation here is a real embrace, not a perfect ending.

how: Christians often read Jacob and Esau's meeting alongside the parable of the prodigal son, and churches use both when teaching about reconciliation between estranged family members.

games.q: you're Esau. the brother who cheated you of your blessing is bowing toward you, seven times, after twenty years. what do you do?
o: make him finish all seven bows, then speak.
run to him, embrace him, and weep.
take his gifts and ride off.
games.why: Esau runs, falls on his neck and kisses him, and they weep. he even tries to refuse the gifts: I have enough, my brother.

practice: Picture someone you've drifted from, or wronged, or been wronged by, and see their face as clearly as you can.

Notice what you expect to find in it, then picture it softening, even a little, and choose one small first step you could take: a text, a wave, a kind word. If you pray, you can pray for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Peniel. The place Jacob named face of God after wrestling there, the same word he uses when he sees that face again in Esau's welcome.

orig.note: Hebrew: face. the same word sits inside Peniel, face of God, where Jacob wrestled the night before.
